                           II.   BACKGROUND                               
21                                                                         
         On November 30, 2021, this Court dismissed claims brought by plaintiffs Coronavirus 
22                                                                         
    Reporter, Calid Inc., Dr. Jeffrey D. Isaacs, and Primary Productions LLC against Apple Inc.  
23                                                                         
    Coronavirus Reporter v. Apple Inc., 2021 WL 5936910 (N.D. Cal. Nov. 30, 2021) (case is 
24                                                                         
    hereafter “Coronavirus I”).  There, the plaintiffs challenged Apple’s alleged “monopolist 
25                                                                         
    operation of its App Store through curation and censorship of smartphone apps.”  Id. at *1 
26                                                                         
    (internal citation omitted) (“Plaintiffs bring this action for antitrust and RICO violations, and 
27                                                                         
    breach of contract and fraud against Apple, Inc…”).  This Court held that the plaintiffs’ antitrust 
1   claims failed because the plaintiffs had failed to define a relevant market or allege an antitrust 
2   injury.  Id. at *6.  This Court dismissed the plaintiffs’ complaint with prejudice because “between 
3   the various iterations of this case being filed across jurisdictions and by different configurations of 
4   Plaintiffs – all challenging the same conduct by Apple and all by the same counsel – this is 
5   Plaintiff’s seventh amended complaint on these claims” and the plaintiffs had still failed to state 
6   any claims.  Id. at *18 (emphasis in original).                       
7        On November 3, 2023, the Ninth Circuit affirmed this Court’s decision.  Coronavirus Rep. 
8   v. Apple, Inc., 85 F.4th 948, 958 (9th Cir. 2023), cert. denied, 144 S. Ct. 2526, 219 L. Ed. 2d 1204 
9   (2024) (holding that “the district court properly dismissed with prejudice all of the claims against 
10   Apple”).  The Ninth Circuit held that “the district court did not abuse its discretion in concluding 
11   that further amendment was not warranted” because “Plaintiffs-Appellants were given a total of 
12   seven opportunities to amend similar complaints across jurisdictions and between various 
13   permutations of plaintiffs, but still failed to state their claims here adequately.”  Id.   
14        On March 3, 2024, the instant Plaintiffs – Coronavirus Reporter Corporation, Calid Inc., 
15   and Greenflight Venture Corporation (“Plaintiffs”) – filed suit against Defendant Apple Inc. in the 
16   District of Wyoming.  Dkt. 1.                                         
17        On July 26, 2024, Plaintiffs filed their First Amended Complaint (“FAC 2”).  Plaintiffs 
18   allege that Apple monopolizes the app distribution market on its devices through its curation and 
19   app approval process for its App Store and suppresses or excludes apps that compete with Apple 
20   or its partners.  Dkt. 30.  Plaintiffs assert nine claims based on this alleged conduct.   
21        On November 21, 2024, the case was transferred to the Northern District of California.  
22   Dkt. 44.                                                              
23        On January 9, 2025, this Court related this case to Coronavirus I.  Dkt. 53.   
24        Defendant filed a motion to dismiss.  Dkt. 62.  It also filed a motion for sanctions against 
25   Plaintiffs under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11, the Court’s inherent authority, and under 28 
26   U.S.C. § 1927.  Dkt. 70.                                              
27        On June 25, 2025, the Court granted Apple’s motion to dismiss (Dkt. 62) because 
1   between Coronavirus I and II and that there was a final judgment on the merits affirmed on 
2   appeal.  The Court held that, as in Coronavirus I, Plaintiffs alleged that Defendant “monopolizes 
3   the app distribution market on its devices through its curation and app approval process for its App 
4   Store” and “that Apple suppresses or excludes apps that compete with Apple or its partners.”  Dkt. 
5   82 at 3.  The Court also found that the parties in both cases were in privity.  In its order dismissing 
6   Plaintiffs’ claims, the Court held that privity was satisfied for the following reasons: 
7                                                                         
              First, Plaintiff Calid Inc. and Defendant Apple “are identical in both 
8             actions.”  Mpoyo v. Litton Electro-Optical Sys., 430 F.3d 985, 988 
              (9th Cir. 2005).                                            
9                                                                         
              Second, Plaintiff Coronavirus Reporter Corporation, a Wyoming C 
10             corporation according to the complaint, was also a party in 
              Coronavirus I.  See Dkt. 30 at ¶ 47.  That the entity includes 
11             “Corporation” in its name in this suit does not render it a new party, 
              particularly where the State of Wyoming has a record of only one 
12             entity including “Coronavirus Reporter” in its name.   See Mot. Exs. 
              1-5.                                                        
13                                                                         
              Finally, the last remaining Plaintiff Greenflight Venture   
14             Corporation is in privity with the plaintiff in the prior case.  “Even 
              when the parties are not identical, privity may exist if ‘there is 
15             substantial identity between parties, that is, when there is sufficient 
              commonality of interest.’”  Tahoe-Sierra Pres. Council, Inc. v. 
16             Tahoe Reg’l Plan. Agency, 322 F.3d 1064, 1081 (9th Cir. 2003) 
              (citing In re Gottheiner, 703 F.2d 1136, 1140 (9th Cir. 1983)).  
17             “Greenflight Venture Corporation” is “Mr. [Jeffrey D.] Isaacs’ 
              solely owned entity.”  Greenflight Venture Corp. v. Google LLC, 
18             765 F. Supp. 3d 1267, 1273 (S.D. Fla. 2025); see Mot. Ex. 6 
              (Florida Secretary of State Corporate Record listing Dr. Jeffrey D. 
19             Isaacs as the Chief Executive Officer of Greenflight Venture 
              Corporation).                                               
20                                                                         
21   Id. at 5 (emphasis and spacing added).1  Thus, Plaintiffs’ claims were barred by res judicata as 
22   there were identical issues in Coronavirus I and II, there was a final judgment on the merits in 
23   Coronavirus I, and the parties in both cases are in privity.          
24        After the Court dismissed Plaintiffs’ claims with prejudice, Plaintiffs filed several motions: 
25   an emergency motion for a temporary stay and status conference (Dkt. 83); a motion for “pre-
26   emptive amicus invitation and limited public-input procedure” (Dkt. 84); an amended version of 
27                                                                         
1   its motion at Dkt. 84 (Dkt. 85); a motion for sanctions against Defendant and Defendant’s counsel 
2   (Dkt. 86); an amended motion to stay “briefing and hearings on Apple’s sanctions motion” and 
3   request to shorten time on Plaintiffs’ motion for a stay (Dkt. 87).  It also filed a motion to relate 
4   cases and for an expedited stay filed before Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers, which Judge 
5   Gonzalez Rogers denied.  Dkts. 89, 93.                                
6        On July 8, 2025, this Court ordered that “Plaintiffs must obtain leave of Court before filing 
7   any additional motions” and that, under Civil Local Rule 7-1(b), the Court would adjudicate 
8   Plaintiffs’ motions without oral argument.  Dkt. 92.                  
9        On July 10, 2025, under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11(c)(3), this Court ordered 
10   Plaintiffs to show cause why their filing of motions (Dkts. 74, 83-87, and 89) did not violate Rule 
11   11(b).  Dkt. 95.  The Court permitted Defendants to file a response to Plaintiffs’ brief.  The parties 
12   filed their respective briefs on this issue on July 14, 2025 and July 17, 2025.  Dkts. 97, 98.   
13        On July 22, 2025, Plaintiffs filed a motion for leave to file a motion for reconsideration of 
14   the Court’s order dismissing Plaintiffs’ claims.  Dkt. 99.            
15        Before the Court are Defendant’s motion for sanctions, responses to the Court’s order to 
16   show cause regarding potential violations of Rule 11 by the Plaintiff, and Plaintiffs’ motions at 
17   Docket Nos. 74, 83-87, and 99.                                        
18     III.  DEFENDANT’S MOTION FOR SANCTIONS AND RESPONSES TO THE         
19                      COURT’S ORDER TO SHOW CAUSE                        
20        Defendant requests that the Court sanction Plaintiffs and Plaintiffs’ counsel under Federal 
21   Rule of Civil Procedure 11, the Court’s inherent authority, or 28 U.S.C. § 1927.  Dkt. 70 at 3.   
22        Further, under Rule 11(c)(3), the Court ordered Plaintiffs to show cause why its filing of 
23   one motion after Defendant filed its motion for sanctions (Dkt. 74) and six motions after the Court 
24   dismissed Plaintiffs’ complaint (Dkts. 83-87, 89) did not violate Rule 11.  Dkt. 95; see Fed. R. 
25   Civ. P 11(c)(3) (“On its own, the court may order an attorney, law firm, or party to show cause 
26   why conduct specifically described in the order has not violated Rule 11(b).”).   
27        For the following reasons, sanctions are warranted.              
1   A.   Rule 11                                                          
2        Sanctions under Rule 11 are warranted because Plaintiffs’ complaint and ensuing motions 
3   are frivolous and lack support in violation of Rules 11(b)(2) and (3).   
4        1.   Legal Standard                                              
5        Rule 11 provides:                                                
6                                                                         
              By presenting to the court a pleading, written motion, or other 
7             paper—whether by signing, filing, submitting, or later advocating 
              it—an attorney or unrepresented party certifies that to the best of the 
8             person’s knowledge, information, and belief, formed after an inquiry 
              reasonable under the circumstances:                         
9                                                                         
              (1) it is not being presented for any improper purpose, such as to 
10             harass, cause unnecessary delay, or needlessly increase the cost of 
              litigation;                                                 
11             (2) the claims, defenses, and other legal contentions are warranted 
              by existing law or by a nonfrivolous argument for extending, 
12             modifying, or reversing existing law or for establishing new law; 
              (3) the factual contentions have evidentiary support or, if 
13             specifically so identified, will likely have evidentiary support after a 
              reasonable opportunity for further investigation or discovery; and 
14             (4) the denials of factual contentions are warranted on the evidence 
              or, if specifically so identified, are reasonably based on belief or a 
15             lack of information.                                        

16                                                                         
    Fed. R. Civ. P. 11(b).  A submission “that does not comply with any one of these requirements 
17                                                                         
    gives grounds for monetary sanctions.”  Lake v. Gates, 130 F.4th 1064, 1068 (9th Cir. 2025) 
18                                                                         
    (affirming district court’s grant of motion for sanctions under Rule 11(b)(3)); see Fed. R. Civ. P. 
19                                                                         
    11(c)(1) and (4).  A court may, on its own, “order an attorney, law firm, or party to show cause 
20                                                                         
    why conduct specifically described in the order has not violated Rule 11.”  Fed. R. Civ. P. 
21                                                                         
    11(c)(3).  A party may also independently move for sanctions against another party for violating 
22                                                                         
    Rule 11 following the procedure outlined in subsection (c)(2).        
23                                                                         
         If “the court determines that [Rule 11] has been violated” after the party or attorney facing 
24                                                                         
    sanctions has had a reasonable opportunity to respond, “the court may impose an appropriate 
25                                                                         
    sanction on any attorney, law firm, or party that violated the rule or is responsible for the 
26                                                                         
    violation.”  Fed. R. Civ. P. 11(c)(1).  “Courts must apply an objective test in assessing whether the 
27                                                                         
    rule has been violated.  A violation of the rule does not require subjective bad faith.”  Yagman v. 
1   Republic Ins., 987 F.2d 622, 628 (9th Cir. 1993) (citations omitted).   
2        2.   Rule 11(b)(2): Frivolous Claims Barred by Res Judicata      
3        Under Rule 11(b)(2), a court may “impos[e] sanctions against [a plaintiff] for [filing] a 
4   frivolous complaint.”  Gaskell v. Weir, 10 F.3d 626, 628 (9th Cir. 1993).  One such example is a 
5   complaint that asserts claims clearly barred by res judicata.  Est. of Blue v. Cnty. of Los Angeles, 
6   120 F.3d 982, 985 (9th Cir. 1997) (“When a reasonable investigation would reveal that a claim is 
7   barred by res judicata or collateral estoppel,” “Rule 11 sanctions may be imposed within the 
8   district court’s discretion.”).  Thus, when a party brings the same “theory to court time after time 
9   and has been told that he is wrong” and asserts the same claims in a new complaint, “the 
10   complaint [is] patently frivolous.”  Roundtree v. United States, 40 F.3d 1036, 1040 (9th Cir. 1994) 
11   (affirming sanctions where an attorney brought the same legal theory to court at least six times and 
12   each court had rejected his theory).                                  
13        Here, Plaintiffs’ complaint is “patently frivolous.”  Id.  As discussed, Plaintiffs’ claims 
14   were barred by res judicata, and any reasonable investigation would have so revealed.   
15        Bringing the instant frivolous case caused needless expenditures by Defendants.  Like the 
16   attorney sanctioned in Roundtree, Dr. Jeffrey Isaacs (through various corporate entities) and his 
17   counsel Mr. Keith Mathews herein have “forced [Apple] to go through essentially the same 
18   expensive exercise; each time [they have] forced courts to adjudicate essentially the same issues.”  
19   Roundtree, 40 F.3d at 1040; see Coronavirus Reporter v. Apple Inc., No. 1:21-cv-00047 (D.N.H.); 
20   Primary Productions LLC v. Apple Inc., No. 2:21-cv-00137 (D. Me.); Coronavirus Reporter v. 
21   Apple Inc., No. 1:21-cv-05567 (N.D. Cal.) (Coronavirus I); Coring Co. v. Apple Inc., No. 9:21-cv-
22   82235 (S.D. Fla.) (collecting Dr. Isaacs’ and Mathews’ other antitrust cases against Apple).  
23   Where parties “attempt[] to have us revisit the claims and theories [repeatedly] rejected,” it 
24   “cannot [be] sa[id] that the district court abuse[s] its discretion when it impose[s] sanctions upon 
25   [such parties].”  Roundtree, 40 F.3d at 1040.  Thus, Plaintiffs and their counsel’s filing of the 
26   frivolous complaint in this case warrants sanctions.                  
27                                                                         
1        3.   Rule 11(b)(2) and (3) Violation: Papers Lacking in Legal and Evidentiary 
2             Support                                                     
3        Further, Plaintiffs’ admission that they used ChatGPT to generate a document submitted 
4   three times to the Court coupled with their submission of motions containing hallucinated citations 
5   violate Rules 11(b)(2) and (3)’s requirement to certify that the “legal contentions are warranted” 
6   and that the “factual contentions have evidentiary support.”  Fed. R. Civ. P. 11.   
7        Specifically, Plaintiffs’ counsel filed a ChatGPT-drafted exhibit, which he submitted to the 
8   Court three times.  Dkt. 97-1 at 9, see Dkts. 84-2 (in support of (“ISO”) motion for “pre-emptive 
9   amicus invitation and limited public-input procedure”), 85-1 (ISO amended version of Dkt. 84), 
10   89-3 (ISO motion to relate cases and for expedited stay before Judge Gonzalez Rogers).  Further, 
11   Plaintiffs filed an anti-SLAPP motion and a response to the Court’s order to show cause that 
12   included hallucinated citations and quotations.  Dkts. 74, 96.        
13        Rule 11 provides, in part, that:                                 
14                                                                         
              By presenting to the court a pleading, written motion, or other 
15             paper—whether by signing, filing, submitting, or later advocating 
              it—an attorney or unrepresented party certifies that to the best of the 
16             person’s knowledge, information, and belief, formed after an 
              inquiry reasonable under the circumstances:…                
17                                                                         
              (2) the claims, defenses, and other legal contentions are warranted 
18             by existing law or by a nonfrivolous argument for extending, 
              modifying, or reversing existing law or for establishing new law; 
19                                                                         
              (3) the factual contentions have evidentiary support or, if 
20             specifically so identified, will likely have evidentiary support after a 
              reasonable opportunity for further investigation or discovery 
21                                                                         
    Fed. R. Civ. P. 11 (emphasis added).  Thus, “Rule 11 imposes a duty on attorneys to certify that 
22                                                                         
    they have conducted a reasonable inquiry and have determined that any papers filed with the court 
23                                                                         
    are well grounded in fact, legally tenable, and not interposed for any improper purpose.”  Cooter 
24                                                                         
    & Gell v. Hartmarx Corp., 496 U.S. 384, 393 (1990).  “The Rule admits of no exceptions to the 
25                                                                         
    requirement that all reasonable attorneys will read a document before filing it in court.”  Zaldivar 
26                                                                         
    v. City of Los Angeles, 780 F.2d 823, 830 (9th Cir. 1986), abrogated on other grounds by Cooter, 
27                                                                         
    496 U.S. 384 (1990).                                                  
1        Here, the Court provided Plaintiffs with an opportunity to show cause why their filing of 
2   motions (Dkts. 74, 83-87, and 89) did not violate Rule 11(b).  Dkt. 95.  In his declaration 
3   supporting Plaintiffs’ response to the order to show cause, Plaintiffs’ counsel admitted that he used 
4   ChatGPT to generate in its entirety an exhibit of a petition seeking “to end Apple’s suppression of 
5   free speech and demand [Apple CEO] Tim Cook’s resignation,” which he submitted to the Court 
6   three times.  Dkt. 97-1 at 9; see Dkts. 84-2, 85-1, 89-3.  Mr. Mathews declares that “the Court 
7   should be aware that no human ever authored the Petition for Tim Cook’s resignation, nor did any 
8   human spend more than about fifteen minutes on it.”  Id.  “[N]o human ever authored the Petition” 
9   because “ChatGPT…created” the Petition in “[t]en minutes.”  Id. at 9-10.  Specifically, as a “legal 
10   experiment,” Mr. Mathews submitted the following prompt to ChatGPT: “Did Judge Gonzales 
11   Rogers’ rebuke of Tim Cook’s Epic conduct create a legally grounded impetus for his termination 
12   as CEO, and if so, write a petition explaining such basis, providing contextual background on 
13   critics’ views of Apple’s demise since Steve Jobs’ death.”  Id.  Mr. Mathews made “minor 
14   corrections” to the Petition, “approved it for distribution,” and requests that the motions it supports 
15   “be granted.”  Id. at 10.  While he attests that he was “surprised at the quality of the work,” Mr. 
16   Mathews does not demonstrate that he “determined that [the] paper[] filed with the court [was] 
17   well grounded in fact, legally tenable, and not interposed for any improper purpose.”  Cooter, 496 
18   U.S. at 393.  Instead, his declaration shows otherwise.  Mr. Mathews describes the 20-page exhibit 
19   that he created and submitted to the Court as a “test” – one that was reviewed in under “fifteen 
20   minutes.”  Dkt. 97-1 at 9.  Thus, Mr. Mathews does not certify that he conducted a “inquiry 
21   reasonable under the circumstances” to determine whether the “factual contentions have 
22   evidentiary support.”  Fed. R. Civ. P. 11(b)(3).                      
23        Moreover, the hallucinated citations and quotations in Mr. Mathews’ motions reveal that 
24   he has likely failed to conduct a “inquiry reasonable under the circumstances” to determine 
25   whether the “legal contentions are warranted by existing law.”  Id. 11(b)(2).  For example, 
26   Plaintiffs’ anti-SLAPP motion contained citations to cases that do not exist (i.e. Klein v. Cheung, 
27   20 Cal. App. 5th 1045 (2018) or direct to different cases or relate to different issues than those 
1   (2018); Atari Interactive, Inc. v. Redbubble, Inc., 2019 WL 6723422 (N.D. Cal. Dec. 10, 2019); 
2   Makaeff v. Trump Univ., LLC, 715 F.3d 254 (9th Cir. 2013)).  See Dkt. 74.  Ironically, Plaintiffs’ 
3   response to the Court’s order to show cause on why they should not be sanctioned includes 
4   hallucinated quotations.  See Dkt. 97 at 6 (citing to Hall v. City of Los Angeles, 697 F.3d 1059, 
5   1067 (9th Cir. 2012) for the quote “issues not decided previously do not become the law of the 
6   case,” when Hall does not include such a quote).  Such “[a]n attempt to persuade a court or oppose 
7   an adversary by relying on fake opinions is an abuse of the adversary system.”  Mata v. Avianca, 
8   Inc., 678 F. Supp. 3d 443, 461 (S.D.N.Y. 2023) (awarding $5000 in sanctions).  Thus, Plaintiffs’ 
9   counsel violated Rule 11 by drafting court documents with ChatGPT without adequate review and 
10   including in his briefs hallucinated cases and quotes.  Mr. Mathews’ violations warrant sanctions 
11   under Rule 11.                                                        
12   B.   Sanctions                                                        
13        Defendant seeks the following sanctions against Plaintiffs and their counsel: 1) $400,000 
14   in joint and several compensatory sanctions; 2) revocation of Mr. Mathews’ pro hac vice 
15   admission; and 3) a pre-filing injunction.  Dkt. 70.                  
16        1.   Legal Standard                                              
17             a.   Procedural Requirements                                
18        Motions for sanctions and orders to show cause why sanctions should not be awarded must 
19   comply with certain procedural requirements.  Motions for sanctions “must not be filed or be 
20   presented to the court if the challenged paper, claim, defense, contention, or denial is withdrawn or 
21   appropriately corrected within 21 days after service or within another time the court sets.”  Fed. R. 
22   Civ. P. 11(c)(2).  Sanctions awarded on the Court’s own initiative must first provide the party 
23   being sanctioned with “notice and a reasonable opportunity to respond.”  Id. 11(c)(1).   
24             b.   Authority to Award Sanctions for Violations            
25        Rule 11(c)(1) provides:                                          
26                                                                         
              If, after notice and a reasonable opportunity to respond, the court 
27             determines that Rule 11(b) has been violated, the court may impose 
              exceptional circumstances, a law firm must be held jointly  
1             responsible for a violation committed by its partner, associate, or 
              employee.                                                   
2                                                                         
3   Fed. R. Civ. P. 11.                                                   
4        2.   Discussion                                                  
5             a.   Procedural Requirements                                
6        First, the procedural requirements are satisfied.  Defendant complied with the 21-day safe 
7   harbor provision by providing Plaintiffs with the requisite documents and providing Plaintiffs with 
8   21 days to withdraw their filings or cure the conduct at issue in its motion for sanctions.  
9   Kleinbrodt Decl. ¶ 12 (Dkt. 70-1 at 5).  Further, in its order requiring that Plaintiffs show cause 
10   why sanctions should be not issued, the Court provided Plaintiffs with notice and an opportunity 
11   to respond to the Court’s order.  See Dkt. 95.                        
12             b.   Appropriate Sanctions                                  
13        Under Rule 11(c)(4):                                             
14                                                                         
              A sanction imposed under this rule must be limited to what  
15             suffices to deter repetition of the conduct or comparable conduct 
              by others similarly situated. The sanction may include      
16             nonmonetary directives; an order to pay a penalty into court; or, if 
              imposed on motion and warranted for effective deterrence, an order 
17             directing payment to the movant of part or all of the reasonable 
              attorney’s fees and other expenses directly resulting from the 
18             violation.                                                  
19   Fed. R. Civ. P. 11 (emphasis added).                                  
20        Here, but for Plaintiffs’ filing of a complaint clearly barred by res judicata and its filing of 
21   numerous unmeritorious motions herein (which the Court summarily denies below), Defendant 
22   would not have had to defend itself in this litigation.  The fees incurred by Defendant in 
23   connection with this litigation are a direct result of the sanctionable conduct found above.  Thus, 
24   Defendant is entitled to the fees and costs reasonably incurred in connection with this litigation.   
25        Defendant shall submit declarations from its attorneys detailing the fee request, and 
26   corresponding time sheets and a brief defining the number of hours of attorney work and 
27   associated costs that Defendant has incurred as a result of Plaintiffs’ sanctionable misconduct.   
1        Defendant effectively asks the Court to find Plaintiffs, Dr. Isaacs (through various 
2   corporate entities), and Mr. Mathews vexatious litigants by requesting a revocation of Mr. 
3   Mathews’ pro hac vice admission and a pre-filing injunction enjoining “Plaintiffs, Mathews, and 
4   Isaacs from suing Apple in any federal court.”  Dkt. 70 at 34.  The Court DENIES this request as 
5   Plaintiffs must be afforded adequate notice and an opportunity to oppose such an order.   
6        A court may declare an individual a vexatious litigant if “(1) the plaintiff is given adequate 
7   notice and an opportunity to oppose the order; (2) the Court compiles an adequate record for 
8   review; (3) the Court makes substantive findings as to the frivolous or harassing nature of the 
9   litigant’s actions; and (4) the order is narrowly tailored ‘to closely fit the specific vice 
10   encountered.’”  Missud v. Nevada, 861 F. Supp. 2d 1044, 1055 (N.D. Cal. 2012), aff'd, 520 F. 
11   App’x 534 (9th Cir. 2013) (quoting Molski v. Evergreen Dynasty Corp., 500 F.3d 1047, 1057 (9th 
12   Cir.2007)).                                                           
13        The third factor requires that the Court “look at ‘both the number and content of the filings 
14   as indicia’ of the frivolousness of the litigant’s claims.”  Molski, 500 F.3d at 1059 (citing De Long, 
15   912 F.2d at 1148).  This factor is satisfied by a finding that a “plaintiff’s claims [are] not 
16   only…numerous, but also…patently without merit.”  Moy v. United States, 906 F.2d 467, 470 (9th 
17   Cir. 1990); see Molski, 500 F.3d at 1059 (finding this factor satisfied because the district court 
18   accurately “conclude[d] that the large number of complaints filed by [the litigant] contain[ed] false 
19   or exaggerated allegations of injury”).                               
20        Should Defendant seek an order declaring Plaintiffs and Dr. Isaacs vexatious litigants, 
21   Defendant shall file a motion to declare them vexatious litigants which addresses all the necessary 
22   elements, provide them with notice, and they shall have an opportunity to be heard by filing their 
23   oppositions to said motion and through a hearing.  See Molski, 500 F.3d at 1057 (“Molski had fair 
24   notice of the possibility that he might be declared a vexatious litigant ... because the district court’s 
25   order was prompted by a motion filed by the defendants and served on Molski’s counsel.  Also, 
26   Molski had the opportunity to oppose the motion, both in writing and at a hearing.”).   
27        Further, the Court notes that “an attorney appearing on behalf of a client cannot be 
1   litigant.”  Weissman v. Quail Lodge, Inc., 179 F.3d 1194, 1197 (9th Cir. 1999). 
2        Thus, Defendant’s request in its motion for sanctions that the Court find the Plaintiffs, Dr. 
3   Isaacs, and Mr. Mathews vexatious litigants is DENIED.  Defendant shall properly initiate the 
4   vexatious litigant process.                                           
5         IV.   PLAINTIFFS’ MOTIONS AT DOCKET NOS. 74, 83-87, AND 99      
6        For the reasons below, Plaintiff’s motions at Docket Nos. 74, 83-87, and 99 are DENIED.   
7   A.   Anti-SLAPP Motion (Dkt. 74)                                      
8        Plaintiffs’ motion to strike Defendant’s motion for sanctions under California’s anti-
9   strategic lawsuit against public participation (“anti-SLAPP) statute (Civil Code of Procedure § 
10   425.16) is denied “[b]ecause a federal court can only entertain anti-SLAPP special motions to 
11   strike in connection with state law claims” and Defendant’s bases to seek sanctions lie in federal 
12   law (Rule 11, a federal court’s inherent authority, and 28 U.S.C. § 1927).  Hilton v. Hallmark 
13   Cards, 599 F.3d 894, 901 (9th Cir. 2010).  Thus, Plaintiffs’ anti-SLAPP motion is DENIED.  
14   B.   Motion for Sanctions (Dkt. 86)                                   
15        Plaintiffs’ motion for sanctions is denied because Plaintiffs failed to comply with Rule 11’s 
16   mandatory 21-day safe-harbor provision.  Under Rule 11(c)(1)(A), a party seeking sanctions is 
17   “required to serve its Rule 11 motion on the [non-moving party] with a demand for retraction of 
18   the allegedly offending allegations, and then to allow the [non-moving party] at least twenty-one 
19   days to retract the pleading before filing the motion with the court.”  Radcliffe v. Rainbow Const. 
20   Co., 254 F.3d 772, 788–89 (9th Cir. 2001).  Where the moving party “d[oes] not comply with the 
21   twenty-one day advance service provision,” that party is “not entitled to obtain an award from the 
22   [non-moving party].”  Id. at 789.  Plaintiffs concede that they have failed to comply with this

6        A court may declare an individual a vexatious litigant if “(1) the plaintiff is given adequate 
7   notice and an opportunity to oppose the order; (2) the Court compiles an adequate record for 
8   review; (3) the Court makes substantive findings as to the frivolous or harassing nature of the 
9   litigant’s actions; and (4) the order is narrowly tailored ‘to closely fit the specific vice 
10   encountered.’”  Missud v. Nevada,
861 F. Supp. 2d 1044, 1055
 (N.D. Cal. 2012), aff'd,
520 F. 11
   App’x 534 (9th Cir. 2013) (quoting Molski v. Evergreen Dynasty Corp.,
500 F.3d 1047, 1057
 (9th 
12   Cir.2007)).                                                           
13        The third factor requires that the Court “look at ‘both the number and content of the filings 
14   as indicia’ of the frivolousness of the litigant’s claims.”  Molski,
500 F.3d at 1059
 (citing De Long, 
15   912 F.2d at 1148).  This factor is satisfied by a finding that a “plaintiff’s claims [are] not 
16   only…numerous, but also…patently without merit.”  Moy v. United States,
906 F.2d 467, 470
 (9th 
17   Cir. 1990); see Molski,
500 F.3d at 1059
 (finding this factor satisfied because the district court 
18   accurately “conclude[d] that the large number of complaints filed by [the litigant] contain[ed] false 
19   or exaggerated allegations of injury”).

22   elements, provide them with notice, and they shall have an opportunity to be heard by filing their

500 F.3d at 1057

14   B.   Motion for Sanctions (Dkt. 86)                                   
15        Plaintiffs’ motion for sanctions is denied because Plaintiffs failed to comply with Rule 11’s 
16   mandatory 21-day safe-harbor provision.  Under Rule 11(c)(1)(A), a party seeking sanctions is 
17   “required to serve its Rule 11 motion on the [non-moving party] with a demand for retraction of 
18   the allegedly offending allegations, and then to allow the [non-moving party] at least twenty-one 
19   days to retract the pleading before filing the motion with the court.”  Radcliffe v. Rainbow Const. 
20   Co.,
254 F.3d 772
, 788–89 (9th Cir. 2001).  Where the moving party “d[oes] not comply with the 
21   twenty-one day advance service provision,” that party is “not entitled to obtain an award from the 
22   [non-moving party].”  Id. at 789.  Plaintiffs concede that they have failed to comply with this 
23   requirement.  Dkt. 86 at 9 (“We candidly note that…a party must serve a [Rule 11] motion and 
24   wait 21 days – but in this case…any such advance notice would only invite further abusive 
25   tactics.”).  Thus, Plaintiffs are “not entitled to obtain an award from” Defendant.  Radcliffe, 254 
26   F.3d at 789.  Plaintiffs’ motion for sanctions is DENIED and, in any event, any such motion 
27   would be frivolous in view of the Court’s findings above.
